checkpoints.section: Why the browser can't tell good scripts from bad
checkpoints.question: Why does the same-origin policy fail to protect against XSS attacks?

options.A: The same-origin policy applies only to cookies and does not control JavaScript execution
options.B: The same-origin policy prevents all scripts from running on any web page
options.C: The same-origin policy only blocks scripts from external domains, but injected scripts already run inside the trusted domain and bypass this protection
options.D: The same-origin policy is enforced by the server and cannot stop attacks on the client

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that the injected script is already inside the trusted domain, so the browser sees it as legitimate and the same-origin policy provides no protection. The policy prevents cross-domain access but does not apply to scripts that are already part of the trusted origin.

checkpoints.question: What is the key difference between reflected XSS and stored XSS?

options.A: Reflected XSS requires users to click a malicious link, while stored XSS is saved in a database and affects all visitors
options.B: Reflected XSS affects only users who click a crafted link, while stored XSS affects every visitor to the page
options.C: Reflected XSS bypasses server-side filters, while stored XSS is caught by input validation
options.D: Reflected XSS is echoed back in an HTTP response, while stored XSS persists in a database

checkpoints.explanation: The section explicitly states that reflected XSS is transient and hits only users who follow the specific link, while stored XSS is saved on the server and served to every visitor. Stored XSS is described as the most dangerous variant because of this widespread impact.

checkpoints.question: Why cannot server-side filtering catch DOM-based XSS?

options.A: DOM-based XSS uses encrypted payloads that bypass server filtering rules
options.B: DOM-based XSS is stored in the browser cache and the server cannot access it
options.C: DOM-based XSS targets HTTP response headers that are processed before validation
options.D: DOM-based XSS occurs entirely in client-side JavaScript and the server never sees the malicious input

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that in DOM-based XSS the server never sees the malicious input because the attack occurs entirely in client-side JavaScript, reading from browser-controlled sources and writing directly to the DOM. This is why server-side filtering cannot catch it.

checkpoints.section: What attackers do once the script runs
checkpoints.question: Which of the following is an immediate goal attackers can achieve by executing JavaScript in an XSS attack?

options.A: Session hijacking by reading the session token from document.cookie and replaying it
options.B: Stealing the victim's credit card number from the server's encrypted vault
options.C: Disabling all network traffic on the victim's device permanently
options.D: Modifying the victim's password in the authentication database directly

checkpoints.explanation: The section explicitly lists session hijacking as one of the first attacks, where the script reads document.cookie to steal the session token and then replays it to impersonate the victim. The other options are outside the scope of what injected JavaScript can accomplish.

checkpoints.question: What is output encoding and where must it happen to prevent XSS?

options.A: Setting the HttpOnly flag on cookies to prevent JavaScript from accessing them
options.B: Validating all user input on the server before storing it in the database
options.C: Converting special characters to safe HTML entities at the point where user data is written into the HTML page
options.D: Implementing a Content Security Policy header to block all external script sources

checkpoints.explanation: The section defines output encoding as converting special characters like `< > & " '` to their safe HTML entity equivalents and states it must happen at the exact point of output. The section notes that encoding rules differ by context, making proper placement critical.

checkpoints.question: How does the HttpOnly cookie flag mitigate XSS attacks?

options.A: It encrypts all cookies so that attackers cannot read their contents even with JavaScript access
options.B: It makes session cookies inaccessible to JavaScript, directly preventing theft via document.cookie
options.C: It expires cookies automatically after each browser session to limit the window of theft
options.D: It blocks cookies from being sent in cross-site requests to prevent credential leakage

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that the HttpOnly cookie flag makes session cookies inaccessible to JavaScript and directly neutralizes the most common XSS goal of session theft via document.cookie.

checkpoints.question: What role does Content Security Policy play as an XSS defense?

options.A: It blocks inline scripts and scripts from unauthorized domains even if injection occurs
options.B: It prevents attackers from stealing session tokens by making cookies inaccessible to scripts
options.C: It is the primary defense that encodes user input before rendering on the page
options.D: It validates all user input before storage to reject malicious payloads

checkpoints.explanation: The section describes CSP as an HTTP response header that tells the browser which script sources are permitted and blocks inline scripts and scripts from unauthorized domains. It is presented as a safety net when encoding is imperfect, rather than the primary defense.
